content:
A 20-year-old co-pilot who earned her private pilot's license at 17, before she had a driver's license, was among the nine people killed when a Learjet 60 crashed in Florida on Sunday, November 1, 2026.

Her name was Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras. Her mother and stepfather confirmed to the New York Post that she was serving as co-pilot aboard the flight.

The aircraft departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.

Around 12:50 p.m. local time, the Learjet 60 crashed in a residential area near Greenacres in Palm Beach County, Florida, the FAA said. All nine people aboard were killed.

Filgueiras grew up in Palm Beach County. She earned her private pilot's license at 17 while attending West Boca Raton High School, before she had obtained a driver's license, according to the Palm Beach Post. Her dream was to become a commercial airline pilot.

Authorities have not released the names of the other eight people aboard. The FAA said the National Transportation Safety Board is in charge of the investigation and will provide updates. The cause of the crash has not yet been determined.

Rest in peace, Nathalia.

Update — November 2, 2026

The families of the seven passengers issued a joint statement on November 2 naming them as Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, their children Emma and Charlie, their friends Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and the children's nanny, Anita Maria Apellido Cetina, the Palm Beach Post and CNN reported. With co-pilot Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras already identified by her family, eight of the nine people aboard have now been publicly identified by family members; authorities have not officially released names. At a November 2 news conference, National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman said there is some evidence the aircraft was breaking up before impact, and that the crew's report of ice and sub-zero temperatures will be a major focus of the inquiry, according to the Palm Beach Post. The crew reported light, clear ice and moderate turbulence, requested to climb 2,000 feet, and declared an emergency as the jet lost altitude, the NTSB said. One person on the ground suffered a minor leg injury from debris, and close to 600 people near the site were temporarily displaced, officials said. The NTSB said it expects to release a preliminary report within 30 days. The cause of the crash has not been determined.

Update — November 3, 2026

At a November 3 news conference, National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman said most of the Learjet's left elevator had been recovered in three pieces between 1.3 and 3.8 miles from the impact site, according to the Associated Press. Investigators had not established whether the separation caused the aircraft to lose control or resulted from forces during the descent, Chapman said. The cause of the crash remains undetermined, and the NTSB still expects a preliminary report within 30 days.

Sources

Federal Aviation Administration statement via UNILAD; New York Post; Palm Beach Post; Palm Beach Post, Nov. 2, 2026; CNN, Nov. 2, 2026. Associated Press, Nov. 3, 2026, via BizJet Journal.
